While the issue was identified and resolved before major rework occurred, it serves as an important reminder for future projects regarding the use of combustible materials in high-rise applications.

actionability.specific_action: Implement a checklist item to verify compliance with NFPA 285 for all exterior wall assemblies over 40' in height.

root_cause_clarity.root_cause: The initial design included combustible materials (gaskets) that did not comply with NFPA 285 standards.

results.question_text: Ref: 1/A8.01, 2/A8.01 For Building 1, the exterior terracotta rainscreen walls are greater than 40’ in height and therefore need to be compliant with NFPA 285 requirements (per CBC 1402.5), which limit the types of combustible materials allowed in the exterior wall assembly. The previously submitted terracotta assembly were believed to be compliant and meet all NFPA 285 requirements, however, upon review it was determined that the wiper gasket at typical terracotta to curtainwall jamb conditions (see detail #1) and the vertical gasket between typical terracotta tiles (see detail #2) are considered combustible and therefore not in compliance with the NFPA standards. Per recent coordination between DES, DPR, and BT Mancini the following proposed modifications were discussed as solutions to have a compliant exterior terracotta assembly: 1) Option #1 – In lieu of the wiper gasket, removing the wiper gasket and installing a black painted metal z- closure 2) Option #2 – In lieu of the vertical gasket, removing the vertical gasket and installed a black painted metal bar An on-site review of the visual mock-up which incorporated the proposed modifications was completed on 09/14/2013 with the DES and DPR team and upon review, DES confirmed that the proposed modifications were acceptable and we were to proceed with these modifications. DPR will proceed off of this confirmation and release BTM to begin finalizing the engineering judgement and resubmitting the terracotta assembly submittal to capture the modifications. Please note these code requirements and modifications do not affect Buildings 2 or PSD as the assemblies are not greater than 40’ in height and the originally intended design are to remain.
results.resolution_text: Julia Morini (DES Architects & Engineers, Inc. - 10012655): Please see attached.

results.question_text: Ref: ERRCS 0.2 (Submittal 0238-283102-0-B1 ERRCS Shop Drawing); E3.01 (B1 PCR #2 dated 01.10.23); E6.01 (B2 50% CD 05.15.23); E3.01, E3.07 (PSD SI-04 dated 06.07.23) Post: E3.01 (B1 PCR #2 dated 01.10.23); detail 1/E6.01 (B2 50% CD 05.15.23); E3.01, E3.07 (PSD SI-04 dated 06.07.23) During talks with the Fire Alarm Vendor, with regards to the heavy space constraints in the B2 Main Electrical Room, they suggested that if a campus-wide fiber optic was utilized with the main ERRCS head-end, located in B1 FCC room (B1 E3.01), and just a smaller VL-RU remote units (see ERRCS 0.2) at each building instead of the bulky head-end units we would get a large space saving. Upon further review with our vendor this option will enable Sprig to fit all equipment in the B2 Main Electrical Room (1/E6.01) without drastic changes to the room itself. However, there are several added benefits of going with this fiber option: 1) Saving space at every location the ERRCS head end equipment would have resided in every building (outside of B1 where the main hub will be) 2) Given the signal strength provided by the fiber optic, all Southline Campus buildings can also utilize this same system as they come online. 3) Only one set of ERRCS antennas on B1 removing the need for antennas on PSD, B2, and future buildings The cost for changing to campus-wide fiber optic ERRCS systems is $8,810 (before markup). Please confirm that this is acceptable.

results.question_text: Reference: SLP1 - RFI0893.2 - B1 Balcony Guardrail Added Plate to Embeds Confirmation_R2 SLP1 - RFI0893.1 - B1 Balcony Guardrail Added Plate to Embeds Confirmation_R1 RFI0893.1-SK5, and SK6 Post on: Detail 8/A8.21 Background: Due to missed steel embeds at corners of Level 3 balcony curbs, the steel embeds for the balcony guardrail were set 1' off of correct locations at the SW and SE balconies. To provide an alternative means of attachment for the balcony guardrails where steel embeds are missing, we propose adding steel plates connected to the steel embeds as noted in the attached sketches. Structural confirmation for the proposed remedial solution was confirmed by Jonathan Chen of DES per response to RFI 0893.1. However, after further evaluation of the originally proposed solution it was determined that a new solution was required due to the limited space between the coping cap from the metal panel and the face of the curb. After reviewing the various options that were discussed, it was decided that the most effective solution would be to add a L5x5 angle where the 1 ½” plate cantilevers, next to the L6x7 angle that will get anchored to the side of the curb. This L5x5 would get anchored down to the SOMD and welded to the bottom of the cantilevered plate. This would occur only at the ends of the curbs where the plate is cantilevered. At the corner’s where we have a column concrete curb, we are proposing to use L5x5 angles to omit the anchor bolts at each plate. The top of the L5x5 would get welded to the bottom of the 1 ½” to provide the support needed. These angles would then get anchored down to the existing column concrete curb. Question: Q1. Please review and confirm the revised proposed sketches SK5 and SK6 (showing the addition of the steel plate per RFI 0893 and omitting the anchors) are acceptable per the attached email with Jonathan Chen/DES.
results.resolution_text: Please see attached.

results.question_text: Reference: SLP1 - RFI0337 - PSD Request to Remove FF/FL Requirements Confirmation Paragraph 3.3J of spec 03 3000 specifies overall FF35/FL25 for slab on grade and FF35 for unshored, supported slabs. 1. The slab on grade slopes between 1% and 2.7% in several directions in order for the water to flow to the drains. Because of this, the FF and FL readings may be inaccurate and therefore we are requesting to remove the FF35/ FL25 requirement on the slab on grade. Please confirm if this is acceptable. 2. The stress on the PT cables can cause the elevated slabs to deflect and curl at the edges. Because of this we are requesting to remove the FF35 requirement from the specification. Please confirm if this is acceptable.
results.resolution_text:
RESPONSE TO Q1: IT IS ACCEPTABLE TO REMOVE FF35/FF25 REQUIREMENTS.
RESPONSE TO Q2: IT IS NOT ACCEPTABLE TO REMOVE FF35 REQUIREMENT, HOWEVER THE MEASUREMENT 
SHOULD BE MEASURED WITHIN 24-72 HOURS AFTER CONCRETE PLACEMENT BEFORE PT STRESSING.
-JASON HSIA (GPLA)

results.question_text: Reference: SLP1 - RFI 1853 - PSD Freas Plastering Water Test Confirmation Southline - PSD Freas Plastering Test Report_20240403 Background: At the parking structure, Freas Plastering installed the approved GE Elemax waterproofing membrane as part of their complete plastering system. In an attempt to ensure that the system is watertight at the NE and NW storage (tiers 3-5), DPR decided to perform a field water test. Due to the project specifications not requiring a field test, DPR performed the test(s) to the best of our ability using the test methods described in the report (ref. attached report). Below is a brief summary of the test procedures and observations that were recorded. During field test #1, there was water intrusion noted within the first two (2) minutes where the face of concrete was flush to face of sheathing. Testing was immediately stopped and DPR performed an investigation on where the water intrusion occurred. As part of remediation efforts, Freas re-applied GE Elemax at the areas where water was noted, and DPR began retesting the location after the Elemax had set (roughly 24 hours after installation). During the second round of testing, water was still identified to be entering at the at the top and bottom corners of the walls. Testing was immediately stopped to begin additional investigation at the locations noted. Freas and DPR began by removing the exterior building paper and lath exposing the waterproofing membrane to ensure that the system was not compromised. With the paper removed, it was noticed that the system was completely dry. Additionally, the team noticed that the leaks were potentially permeating through the concrete adjacent to the plaster walls. Since the system was completely dry, Freas did not reapply any additional waterproofing. A third test was performed after the location had dried up from the previous test (roughly 24-48 hours). For the third round of testing, it was decided to test the system from inside of the storage rooms to isolate the plaster system from the concrete where the walls abut to. When the water was being spray from the inside, no water intrusion could be visible from the outside where the waterproofing was installed. However, when water was sprayed beyond the plaster walls, water intrusion was observed from the outside at the concrete cracks and voids.
